(CNN)  -- Over 28,000 Liverpool fans marked the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster in a special memorial service at Anfield on Wednesday. Liverpool supporters at the Kop end paid their respects in an emotional afternoon at Anfield. A total of 96 supporters died on April 15, 1989 before the FA Cup semifinal between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Sheffield Wednesday's stadium, the worst-ever tragedy in English sporting history. To commemorate the anniversary, the city of Liverpool came to a standstill at 3.06 pm (1406 GMT) with the bells of the two cathedrals and its civic buildings ringing out in memory of those fans who lost their lives. On Anfield's famous Kop, 96 candles were lit while commemorations took place at Hillsborough and also in Nottingham. Members of the current Liverpool team stood somberly as hymns were played before a roll call of the dead was read out. Club legend Kenny Dalglish, who was Liverpool manager at the time of the disaster, then read a short prayer. The mayor of Liverpool, Steve Rotherham, who was at the game 20 years ago, helped organize the emotional memorial. "Hillsborough affected so many lives, not just on Merseyside but across the whole of the UK," he said. "I attended the match 20 years ago and the passing years do not diminish the importance and the poignancy of this occasion." Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard, whose 10-year-old cousin Jon-Paul Gilhooley was the youngest victim of the tragedy, spoke of his feelings this week. "Time has gone by, but the scars will never ever be healed and the fans will never ever forget. So you can always rely on our supporters to be there for you when you need them." The Liverpool fans died in a crush which started just before the kick-off as the gate at the Leppings Lane End was opened with terrible consequences. The match started but when the scale of the tragedy became clear, it was swiftly abandoned at 3.06 pm. In the immediate aftermath, the British government commissioned Lord Justice Taylor to conduct an inquiry which would have a far-reaching impact on football. Taylor was deeply critical of the police operation at Hillsborough, but his most significant recommendations were the removal of perimeter fencing and the creation of all-seater stadia. His report also cleared Liverpool fans of blame for the tragedy after lurid tabloid headlines provoked revulsion on Merseyside. Prime minister Gordon Brown paid reference to the controversy in an interview released on Liverpool's official television channel. "It was wrong for people to blame, as some did, Liverpool fans on that day," he said. "That's probably what matters most -- that people understood that the behavior of Liverpool fans in helping each other was magnificent. "Let's never forget the fans who cruelly lost their lives on a day when we know the people of Liverpool were trying to help each other," he added. However, the people of Liverpool are still angry and bitter at the lack of justice for those who died -- and that frustration surfaced when Andy Burnham, the   Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport took to the stand to address the crowd. As Burnham spoke, the crowd rose as one to sing "Justice for the 96". The Kop chant boomed around the stadium and Burnham, an Everton fan, was left in no doubt about the strength of feeling over the lack of accountability from officialdom over the tragedy. Fittingly, the ceremony was concluded with Gerry Marsden leading the fans in singing Liverpool anthem 'You'll Never Walk Alone'.

Two decades after the fatal crush on the overcrowded Leppings Lane terrace, the pain remained raw, but the resolve of the families and survivors was stronger than ever.

At precisely 3:06 p.m.—the exact time the fatal match was stopped 20 years ago—the city of Liverpool fell silent. At Anfield, the home of Liverpool Football Club, heads bowed in a chilling, powerful minute of silence broken only by the quiet sobs of mourners. 

As the silence ended, a church bell tolled 96 times, once for each man, woman, and child who went to a football match and never came home. For each toll, a candle was lit on the pitch around a mosaic reading "96."

### A Demand for Justice

While the service was a time for grief and remembrance, it also served as a fiery political rallying point. 

The lingering anger over the official handling of the disaster, the original inquest verdicts of "accidental death," and the smear campaigns orchestrated by police and parts of the media in the aftermath boiled over during a speech by UK Culture Secretary Andy Burnham.

As Burnham began to deliver a message on behalf of Prime Minister Gordon Brown, his speech was interrupted by a spontaneous, deafening roar from the Kop grandstand. Tens of thousands of people stood to chant in unison: *"Justice for the Ninety-Six! Justice for the Ninety-Six!"*

The chanting continued for over two minutes, forcing a visibly shaken Burnham to pause. 

"I heard you loud and clear today," Burnham eventually told the crowd, promising to pass their demands for full disclosure of government and police documents to the highest levels of parliament.

### A City United

The disaster fundamentally changed the face of modern football, leading to the Taylor Report, which mandated all-seater stadiums across top-tier English football. But in Liverpool, the legacy of Hillsborough is defined by solidarity.

### The Long Fight Continues

For the families of the victims, the 20th anniversary marked both a painful milestone and a testament to their endurance. Many of the bereaved have spent two decades campaigning against what they view as a massive establishment cover-up that blamed innocent fans for the overcrowding.

Trevor Hicks, who lost his two teenage daughters, Sarah and Vicki, in the disaster and serves as a spokesman for the Hillsborough Family Support Group, expressed gratitude for the unwavering support of the city.

"Twenty years is a long time," Hicks said. "We are older, we are tired, but we are as determined as ever. The truth is out there, and we will not stop until we have justice."

As the two-hour service drew to a close, local singer Kenny Parry led the stadium in a rendition of Liverpool’s anthem, "You’ll Never Walk Alone."

**A City United in Grief and Grace: Remembering Hillsborough 20 Years On**

On April 15, 2009, time stood still in Liverpool. Exactly twenty years after Britain’s worst sporting disaster, tens of thousands gathered at Anfield stadium, while an entire city paused to honor the 96 men, women, and children who lost their lives at the Hillsborough football stadium in 1989. 

The 2009 memorial service was not merely an act of solemn remembrance; it was a monumental display of community solidarity, a poignant reminder of deep-seated trauma, and ultimately, a fierce catalyst for a truth that had been denied for two decades.

---

### The Day the World Stopped: April 15, 1989

To understand the raw emotion of the 2009 service, one must look back to the sunny spring afternoon that changed British football forever. On April 15, 1989, Liverpool FC faced Nottingham Forest in the FA Cup semi-final at the neutral Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield. 

Thousands of Liverpool supporters traveled to Yorkshire, buzzing with anticipation. However, gross mismanagement by South Yorkshire Police and fatal flaws in crowd control led to catastrophe. To ease congestion outside the Leppings Lane turnstiles, South Yorkshire Police Commander David Duckenfield ordered a large exit gate (Gate C) to be opened. 

An estimated 2,000 fans poured through the gate, unknowingly funneling down a narrow tunnel directly into the already overcrowded central pens 3 and 4 behind the goal. Trapped against the steel perimeter fences that had been installed to prevent pitch invasions, fans were crushed to death. Ninety-six supporters lost their lives—ranging in age from 10-year-old Jon-Paul Gilhooley to 67-year-old Gerard Baron—and hundreds more were injured.

In the tragic aftermath, police authorities and sections of the media falsely attempted to blame the fans, alleging drunkenness and disorder. For the families of the victims, the pain of losing loved ones was compoundingly exacerbated by a decades-long smear campaign and a cover-up by state institutions.

---

### The Legacy of the Taylor Report

In the wake of the disaster, the British government appointed Lord Justice Taylor to conduct an inquiry into the events. Published in 1990, the **Taylor Report** was a landmark document that dismantled the false narratives surrounding fan behavior.

Taylor concluded that the main cause of the disaster was a failure of police control. Crucially, the report stated that fan unruliness played no role in the tragedy. 

Beyond assigning fault, the Taylor Report revolutionized the landscape of modern sports architecture. Its recommendations transformed football stadia across the United Kingdom:
* **Elimination of Standing Terraces:** Top-tier clubs were required to convert their grounds into all-seater stadiums.
* **Removal of Perimeter Fencing:** The dangerous steel cages surrounding pitches were pulled down, ensuring fans could escape onto the field in an emergency.
* **Modernized Safety Standards:** Alcohol bans near pitches, improved CCTV, and upgraded turnstile technology were implemented nationwide.

While the Taylor Report permanently changed British football for the safer, it did not lead to immediate criminal prosecution for those responsible, leaving the bereaved families with an unfulfilled quest for justice.

---

### Anfield, 2009: A Resounding Cry for Justice

By the time the 20th anniversary arrived in 2009, the grief had not diminished, but the resolve of the city had hardened. Over 30,000 people crammed into the stands at Anfield—filling the Kop, the Main Stand, and the Centenary Stand—to pay their respects. 

The atmosphere was electric with emotion. Ninety-six candles were lit on the pitch, surrounding a temporary memorial structure. As the names of the 96 victims were read aloud, a bell tolled for each soul lost, cutting through the heavy silence of the stadium.

A turning point in the long struggle for justice occurred during the service. When the Culture Secretary, Andy Burnham, rose to speak on behalf of the British government, he was interrupted by a spontaneous, thunderous chant from the crowd: *"Justice for the 96!"* 

The chant echoed off the roofs of Anfield for several minutes. It was a visceral, powerful moment that brought the government to a stark realization: two decades later, Liverpool would not let this rest. Shocked by the raw pain and anger of the crowd, Burnham returned to London determined to act. This moment directly catalyzed the creation of the Hillsborough Independent Panel, which eventually led to the quashing of the original inquest verdicts and the full exoneration of the fans in 2016.

The service concluded with a heartbreakingly beautiful rendition of Liverpool FC’s anthem, *"You’ll Never Walk Alone,"* sung by soprano Natasha Marsh alongside thousands of tearful attendees, their scarves held high in the air.

---

### A City Brought to a Halt

Beyond the walls of Anfield, the entire city of Liverpool observed the anniversary with unprecedented reverence, demonstrating a remarkable unity that transcended traditional football rivalries.

At **3:06 PM**—the exact time the match was halted on that fateful day in 1989—the city paused:
* **Traffic Came to a Standstill:** Buses, cars, and trains stopped. Mersey Ferries blew their horns in tribute as they idled on the river.
* **Bells Tolled:** The bells of Liverpool Cathedral, the Metropolitan Cathedral, and the Town Hall rang out 96 times.
* **A Minute’s Silence:** Shops closed their doors, construction sites fell silent, and workers stood on streets throughout the city center, heads bowed.
* **United Across the Divide:** Everton FC, Liverpool's fierce local rivals, stood shoulder-to-shoulder with their neighbors. Everton manager David Moyes and players attended services, emphasizing that the tragedy was not a red or blue issue, but a Mersey issue.

Flags flew at half-mast from public buildings, and the public laid thousands of floral tributes, scarves, and handwritten notes at the memorial outside Anfield and in the city center.

---

### The Unbroken Spirit

The 2009 Hillsborough memorial service was a watershed moment. It honored the memory of 96 innocent fans whose lives were cut short while simply going to watch a football match. But more than that, it demonstrated the unbreakable spirit of a city that refused to let its loved ones be forgotten or blamed for their own deaths.

As the thousands filed out of Anfield on that April afternoon in 2009, the message left behind was clear: the 96 would always be remembered, and Liverpool would never walk alone in its pursuit of the truth.
